title: BioWare veteran says Baldur's Gate 3 was such a great sequel because it didn't try to be too much like Baldur's Gate 2
author: Andy Chalk
text:
Mark Darrah was a programmer on the original Baldur's Gate and Baldur's Gate 2, along with Neverwinter Nights and Jade Empire, and served as executive producer of the Dragon Age series from Origins through Inquisition before leaving in 2020—and coming back in 2023 to kick in on The Veilguard. He knows a thing or two about BioWare RPGs, in other words, and speaking to FRVR he said he also knows why Baldur's Gate 3 was such a great sequel—so great that it has overshadowed the games that came before it, made mounts of money, and is still among the most popular games on Steam three years after release.
Darrah reckons that's a direct result of Larian's willingness to do its own thing with the sequel. Obsidian's Pillars of Eternity "feels like an Infinity Engine game," Darrah said (and he's 100% correct on that), and they're great, but Darrah says that's also a very limiting factor: "The reality is that the industry has moved on so much since then that I was like, oh yeah, this is a really faithful adaptation of that and it turns out that I didn’t actually want that anymore."
Larian, on the other hand, "are Baldur’s Gate 2 and Baldur’s Gate 1-flavoured, but they’re also Divine Divinity-flavoured. They are flavoured by their own track record, they are flavoured by what CRPGs have become in the intervening 20 years. So I think it’s a great sequel. I think they did what is the right thing to do given that large of a gap."
Baldur's Gate 3 really is more akin to Larian's Divinity games than its namesakes, and those Divinity games are brilliant RPGs too. Original Sin 2 took our Game of the Year crown in 2017: PC Gamer's Wes Fenlon said at the time that "there's never been an RPG with a story or characters this interesting that you can play co-op with four players," which is also a pretty spot-on description of Baldur's Gate 3.
The problem for Baldur's Gate owner Hasbro is that Larian's work was maybe a little too great: The company now finds itself in possession of a massively lucrative videogame property that nobody wants to touch because, basically, who wants to go on after The Beatles? Darrah has thoughts on that too—basically, do a Fallout: New Vegas with it.
"Get Larian to agree to license out the Divinity Engine and essentially let someone make an oversized expansion pack for Baldur’s Gate 3 and call that Baldur’s Gate 4," Darrah said. "That could work."
Conversely, it could take the approach suggested by PC Gamer editor Fraser Brown: Just don't.

title: From ancient Buddhism, to iconic manga hair, to Keanu Reeves: a PC Gamer Causality Chain™
author: Wes Fenlon
text:
Causality Chain is a series at PC Gamer exploring the unlikely links between history, culture, and videogames. And ocassionally hedgehogs.
The arc of history curves in mysterious ways. Beloved actor Keanu Reeves—Ted, Neo, John Wick himself—may not be Buddhist , but he does, in fact, owe the existence of one of his blockbuster roles to the teachings of one of Buddhism's most important figures.
How, you ask? And what exactly does this have to do with videogames? Excellent questions that can only be answered by a causality chain, tracing the butterfly effect of a man walking westward 1,400 years ago to the modern day movie star known for his iconic delivery of the word "Whoa."
Join us, as we tip over the dominoes to link past to present...
The origins of Chinese Buddhism 🔗 Keanu Reeves big dogging Sonic the Hedgehog
The foundational text
🧵Unspool🧵
620s AD: Around the year 627, Chinese Buddhist monk Xuanzang begins a 17 year journey from China to India in search of Buddhist texts...
He returns in the year 645 with hundreds of Sanskrit manuscripts, which he will work to translate until his death. One of Xuanzang's disciples writes and publishes a book titled Records of the Western Regions, a dictated account of his pilgrimage. 1
(Image credit: Wikimedia)
A legendary journey
🧵Unspool🧵
1590s: Xuanzang's account inspires 1,000 years of folktales, both written and in the oral tradition. In the late 16th century, a fictional account of the journey of Buddhist monk Tang Sanzang and the monkey king Sun Wukong is published under the name Journey to the West. 2
(Image credit: Wikimedia)
From the west to the east
🧵Unspool🧵
1984 : Manga artist Akira Toriyama decides to follow up his hit comic Dr. Slump, which was set in a vague satirical version of America, with a new series that has "Chinese scenery" instead. 3
Toriyama uses Journey to the West as the template, saying in a 1995 interview "I thought it would be easy if that story served as the basis, since all I would have to do would be to arrange things." His protagonist Son Goku is modeled after the Monkey King.
(Image credit: Akira Toriyama, Jump)
The Super moment
🧵Unspool🧵
1991: After Dragon Ball becomes increasingly popular as a battle manga, Toriyama gives Goku a power-up called Super Saiyan. He draws Super Saiyan Goku with a golden aura and blonde hair instead of black so that his assistant can spend less time inking Goku's hair each issue. 4
(Image credit: Akira Toriyama, Shueisha)
Sonic's power-up looks mighty familiar
🧵Unspool🧵
1992: Sonic the Hedgehog 2 debuts in November the following year. When he powers up by collecting the Chaos Emeralds, Sonic glows gold and transforms into Super Sonic.
Coincidence?? No. 5
(Image credit: Sega)
Sonic needs a shadow
🧵Unspool🧵
2001: To give Sonic a more powerful rival, Sonic Team creates Shadow the Hedgehog, the "ultimate lifeform." He canonically approves of stealing candy from babies 6 , and is also maybe Vegeta. 7
(Image credit: Sega)
Keanu is the ultimate life form?
🧵Unspool🧵
2024: After being cast as the voice of Shadow, Keanu Reeves looks an interviewer dead in the eyes and declares that he, either as a human man or the voice of a CGI hedgehog, can beat up Sonic the Hedgehog. 8
(Image credit: Keanu Reeves, Paramount)

title: FromSoftware sleuth unearths earliest footage of Demon's Souls to date: A prototype with a first person camera mode
author: Ted Litchfield
text:
Seasoned FromSoftware investigator Lance McDonald has shared a recently uncovered early internal showcase of Demon's Souls , FromSoft's crucial pivot point between King's Field and Dark Souls, and the progenitor of its own subgenre.
The demonstration consists of a PowerPoint presentation deck and early gameplay trailer. It was shown at "Gameshare 4," an internal Sony event held in May, 2007, almost two years before Demon's Souls' initial release in Japan.
The real highlight is that two minute gameplay showcase, possibly the earliest look we've ever gotten of Demon's Souls in action, with key differences from the final game. First and most striking: There are a few sequences in a first-person camera mode à la King's Field, FromSoft's spiritual predecessor to Souls. It makes for a distinct minority of the footage's runtime, and seems to have been an optional mode you were meant to toggle between.
It also ties into what strikes me as an equally profound, but less immediately grabbing difference: Demon's Souls' early 3D camera was locked behind the player model, which always faced away from the camera⁠—it reminds me of the Jedi Knight games, for a frame of reference.
This would have complimented the first person mode better than the final camera, but it would have also made for a radically different overall experience. The Souls series of today is defined by a camera that can freely rotate around the player and lock onto enemies⁠—it's the bedrock of the games' positioning-based combat.
The demo takes place in an early version of Demon's Souls' tutorial area. The Vanguard Demon is shown in his same arena, practically unchanged compared to the final game⁠—indeed, his moveset and animations have survived all the way to Elden Ring with the Erdtree Avatars.
The Dragon God's arena is open-air in this version, a volcanic crater instead of the magma cavern of the final game. The trailer also features enemies not seen in Demon's Souls' release version: Bipedal snake men resembling the man-serpents of Dark Souls. FromSoft loves revisiting a motif.
There are plenty of interesting nuggets in the PowerPoint as well, read in the video by John Linneman of Digital Foundry. Here's what stood out to me:
Some striking concept art, including the Flamelurker boss and an open, grassy area with a weird, big hole at the center⁠—the ominous valley and strange rock formations weirdly remind me of the fingerprint ruins from Elden Ring: Shadow of the Erdtree.
FromSoft and Sony clearly felt Demon's Souls' asymmetric multiplayer was its ace in the hole (and/or potentially confusing), and spent a lot of runtime explaining it.
They presented it as a midpoint between MMOs and pure singleplayer games, joking that it would destroy your life less than the former (complete with a reference to South Park's "Make Love, Not Warcraft").
A real "Oh, bless their hearts" development roadmap that predicted completion in June, 2008. Demon's Souls launched in Japan in February '09.
Repeated references to a "worldwide release," underlining the bad feelings that must have resulted over Sony only publishing Demon's Souls in Japan .
Overall, what was at the time an anodyne bit of internal corporate communication is now an invaluable piece of videogame history. Demon's Souls was a crucial transition game that could have just as easily become a fondly-remembered but little-played cult classic.
It almost didn't make it to America and Europe, and there was no guarantee that it would prove one of the most influential games on the coming decade. Now we understand how close it was to being a very different experience.

title: GTA 6's Netflix deal forces us to ask: can you pirate an advertisement?
author: Tyler Wilde
text:
Let's be real, come August 27, the Grand Theft Auto 6 "extended look" is not going to be exclusive to Netflix for six hours as advertised. It's going to be exclusive to Netflix for however long it takes for someone to record it and distribute a torrent.
You wouldn't download a car, but would you download an ad for a game about stealing cars?
It would be, I've now had to consider, technically piracy to do so. After all, Netflix probably paid good money for the privilege of being the first to show the world GTA 6 gameplay, although we can only guess, because the financial terms of the deal haven't been disclosed.
Aside from whatever funds exchanged hands, GTA publisher Take-Two's motivation for the deal is to signal that GTA 6 is a cultural event that transcends the gaming scene. And Netflix gets to be associated with that cultural event.
I get Netflix's angle. I don't get Take-Two's, unless the payday was astronomical. Everyone already knows GTA is a big deal, and it's plain disrespectful to GTA fans to turn the gameplay trailer they've been waiting for into a money-making opportunity, especially given that many of them have already pre-ordered the game.
Having to wait six hours to watch a trailer is a relatively minor inconvenience, all things considered, but monetizing a trailer is just tacky. It certainly doesn't reinforce Take-Two CEO Strauss Zelnick's claim that GTA 6 is an "incredible bargain" at $80-$100. It suggests, instead, that we should brace for maximum nickel-and-diming and FOMO exploitation.
I suppose this is how it goes when you don't have to worry about your reputation. There's not much Take-Two and Rockstar could do to hurt GTA 6's sales at this point: They've already sold a zillion pre-orders (or something like that) without any gameplay trailer at all. If there is a line that can't be crossed, it's a couple celestial bodies removed from a tacky gameplay reveal or a new labor scandal.
When the GTA 6 extended look debuts on Netflix on August 27, we'll watch it and report on its contents here, but I imagine a quick scan of social media will allow you to illicitly experience the marketing beat early, if you're the sort of outlaw who dares to watch pirated videogame trailers.

title: Big Walk: So, what's the deal with that number puzzle?
author: Christopher Livingston
text:
Early on in Big Walk, as you and your pals are scurrying around the world solving puzzles, you might come across a curious sight: a structure near the beach with an oblong prize (here at PC Gamer we call it a nubbin ) inside a frosted glass container. Hanging on a hook above it: a sign with some numbers on it. Curious!
You've probably already seen a nubbin in a similar container, which could only be accessed when one of your companions held down a button in a nearby location. But what do these two four-digit numbers mean? And where's the button?
(Image credit: Panic) If you're stumped with this numbers puzzle, as we were for a while, we're happy to help.
Since Big Walk is best when you figure puzzles with your friends instead of by reading guides, I'll ease you into the solution to this number puzzle by giving you progressively more explicit hints below. This way you can get some help without completely spoiling the solution, if you like.
Hints
Hint 1 :
When you first find this number puzzle, most likely just after you've completed the tutorial puzzles, you won't be able to solve it. It's just that simple. The best advice is to leave it for now and come back to it later, after you've solved five other puzzles and completed the red tower.
Hint 2 :
When you're looking around the rest of the world, keep those numbers in mind. Specifically, the format: two four-digit numbers. Maybe you'll see something elsewhere that looks like it's related.
Hint 3 :
You'll need a specific item to make sense of those numbers. There are actually two different items that can be individually used to help you with the number puzzle.
Hint 4 :
The numbers 4166 and 1899 are coordinates, latitude and longitude, and they point to the button's location on the island.
Hint 5 :
There's a map that can be used to find the coordinates, and there's a device that displays its current coordinates on a screen, like a GPS. Either of those can be used to solve the number puzzle.
OK, that's enough hints. Here's the solution:
Solution
First, you can find the map, which requires placing five nubbins on the red tower's roof. The map room will then open up right next to the starting hub, which features a large map on the floor, and a portable, foldable map and compass.
With the map opened in your hands, you can follow the longitude (the numbered lines on the sides) of 41 and the latitude (the numbered lines on the top and bottom) of 18. Where they meet on the map is the grid square to search for the button, which is east and south of the starter hub. The "66" in 4166 refers to a more exact measurement than the map shows, meaning it's about two-thirds of the way south from the top of the grid, and 99 means it's about as far east as you can be in the grid, right along the gridline.
Enlarge the image below by clicking on the arrows on the lower-left corner, if it helps.
(Image credit: Panic) That's where to look! You'll find a small button carefully camouflaged behind a rock. Someone will have to hold down the button while another player grabs the nubbin at that puzzle building when the glass container opens, so make sure you've got walkie-talkies with you.
The other way to find the button (and the more fun way, in my opinion) is by using the GPS device. This item will take longer to find than the map: you'll need to visit the green tower, which is in the same area you'll eventually find the button, and just outside it you'll see a red frame holding the GPS (and another sign with more numbers on it).
(Image credit: Panic) You can hold the GPS up to friends to show current coordinates, or stick it on someone's backpack.
With one player wearing the GPS on their back, another player can direct them which way to go. Just keep your eyes on the numbers: as you move across the island, the GPS readout will tell you if you're getting closer or further from the location of the button. Happy walking!

title: Tencent's cyberpunk rival to Grand Theft Auto is in trouble as its developer lays off 80 people
author: Rick Lane
text:
Tencent's ambitious attempt to build a rival to Grand Theft Auto appears to be floundering, as Last Sentinel developer Lightspeed LA has laid off 80 people following the publisher's loss of confidence in the project.
If you're not familiar with Last Sentinel, that would be forgivable. The cyberpunk open world has been in development for six years and was announced at The Game Awards in 2023. But doubts began to circulate about the state of the Last Sentinel after a suite of promotional videos published last year failed to show any footage of the game itself.
Now, as reported by Bloomberg , it appears we'll be lucky to see any of Last Sentinel at all. Following multiple delays and at least one partial project reboot, publisher Tencent has opted not to move forward with the project, and as a result Lightspeed Entertainment has laid off dozens of employees.
As Bloomberg details, Last Sentinel appears to have been in trouble for some time. The game was built as a glossy open-world affair set in a vertical city in a cyberpunk Japan, featuring destructible environments alongside the usual GTA-ish mix of driving and shooting.
However, the game was being built by a much smaller team than Rockstar used for its latter-day open worlds, and according to anonymous sources at Lightspeed, that team had to contend with an unclear vision and a "polarizing" approach to management by former Rockstar San Diego studio director Steve Martin.
After a poor playtest and an unimpressive demonstration to Tencent executives earlier this year, Lightspeed apparently scrambled to assemble an improved version of Last Sentinel. But whatever the team put together apparently wasn't enough, and Tencent has washed its hands of the project.
To be clear, Last Sentinel hasn't been cancelled yet . Lightspeed is still working on the project without Tencent's backing. But the studio is planning to "shift the creative and development direction" of the game "to meet player expectations". Given players were set up to expect a cyberpunk open-world rival to Grand Theft Auto, it's hard to see how Lightspeed can square this given the challenges that lie ahead.

title: God of War TV series sees further recasts as Amazon seeks older actors for Atreus and Thrud
author: Rick Lane
text:
Amazon's God of War series has already seen one major recast , with Kratos actor Ryan Hurst having to depart the role after suffering a bicep tear on set. While Hurst has reportedly had surgery and is recovering, the injury was severe enough that production was paused and Amazon has opted to seek out a replacement. Dave Bautista is apparently in talks to replace him.
But Kratos isn't the only character in the TV show who will be seeing a change in actor. Amazon also plans to recast roles of Atreus and Thrud. Unlike Kratos' impromptu recasting, however, the switch for these characters is a planned, creative decision that will take effect from Season 2 onward.
In Season 1, Atreus and Thrud are played by child actors Callum Vinson and Island Austin. But as reported by mp1st , casting calls for Season 2 suggest these characters will be significantly older when that second season rolls around. The casting calls for both characters (who have the codenames 'Joshua' and 'Ruth') to be "Teen" versions, while Joshua's casting call states that in Season 2 Kratos' son "finds his new identity and grows into manhood."
The new casting also implies that Season 2 will roll straight into the events of God of War: Ragnarök rather than splitting the first game into multiple arcs of television. Both seasons are being produced back-to-back, with production originally planned to wrap in April 2027. Whether or not this will be affected by the ongoing hiatus is unclear, as production is not expected to resume until October.
As for who will be playing Kratos instead of Hurst, there are reports Dave Bautista is "in talks" to step into the role. Presumably, Bautista would be more expensive to cast than Hurst. But this is Amazon we're talking about.
At least by the time the God of War show launches, they'll have a third season of material to film. The next game in the series, God of War: Laufey , is due to launch in February next year. Sadly, it isn't coming to PC , as PlayStation has sworn off launching games on the platform for the time being. I'm curious to see how long this lasts, given how much money Sony made by releasing its PlayStation exclusives on PC thus far.

title: Blocky zombie survival sim Unturned releases its source code so players can build a 'lasting legacy' for the game 'regardless of the changes we make'
author: Rick Lane
text:
Smartly Dressed Games, developer of the wildly popular free-to-play zombie survival sim Unturned, has released the game's source code for non-commercial use.
"Unturned's source code and project files are now freely available!" the developers wrote in a Steam post . "Whether you have a new feature or total conversion in mind, the sky's the limit."
The source code is available via GitHub . In an accompanying FAQ , Smartly Dressed Games explained that the reason behind the release is to further support the community's creative efforts.
"Unturned's greatest strength is our passionate community," the studio wrote. "Releasing the source files allows you and other players to further expand upon the game as you see fit, building a lasting legacy for the game regardless of the changes we make or how many years pass."
There are some conditions for players and modders who want to use the source code. In the FAQ, Smartly Dressed Games stressed that uses for the source code "must be strictly non-commercial" and that "players must be able to play and access all features and content of your mod for free." Some elements of code have also been removed from the game because Smartly Dressed Games doesn't have the rights to redistribute it, such as code relating to anti-cheat systems and third-party pathfinding programs.
The developers also note that the source code release does not mean that Unturned itself is open source, as the non-commercial license does not meet the Open Source Initiative's definition of the term. It is something that Smartly Dressed Games would like to do in the future. title: Golden Sun Is One of the Best RPGs Ever Made — and the Last of Its Kind
author: Josh Broadwell
text: They just don't make games like Golden Sun anymore. After Camelot and Nintendo released the much-lauded RPG for the Game Boy Advance in August 2001, the genre began a slow decline both in volume and innovation. The genre shrank, and its eventual regrowth, in trying too hard to recapture past glories, has largely fallen short. Which is a shame. Golden Sun deserves every bit of praise heaped on it, as one of the only examples of a modern (at the time) RPG that built on its inspirations and turned them into something wholly new and captivating.
